query: Consider the following context: How to rationally design composition of alloys with desired properties has always been an open and challenging question, especially for high-entropy alloy (HEA) which has huge selections of composition due to the feature of multi-principal elements. Although great efforts have been made in the past decades, such as approaches based on thermo-kinetic analysis and simulations, strategies to quick determine the optimal HEA composition remain lacking. In that context, which method can be used for design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight refractory HEA (RHEA) compositions, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-throughput composition design method that combines computational thermodynamic screening (e.g., CALPHAD‐based modeling) with a high‐entropy alloy design framework can identify refractory HEA compositions that intrinsically balance high strength, ductility, and low density. This method works by pinpointing alloy formulations where the multi‐principal elements induce a disordered BCC (or near‐BCC) matrix with tailored lattice distortions and controlled precipitate formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys based on multiple refractory elements (e.g., W, Mo, Ta, Nb) without optimized low-mass alloying additions.
generation.intervention: Apply high-throughput computational screening (using CALPHAD or similar thermodynamic models) to explore the vast composition space of refractories in HEAs, then experimentally validate candidate compositions with low-weight alloying additions.
generation.conditions: The design process is performed under assumptions of both room temperature and elevated temperature (up to 1000°C or above) service, replicating the severe operating conditions required for high-performance structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A disordered, possibly BCC-dominated microstructure with controlled lattice distortion and, where beneficial, fine-scale coherent precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The intrinsic lattice distortions from mixing multiple elements impede dislocation motion for strength, while the controlled alloying (including low-density additions) optimizes ductility and reduces overall weight. The high-throughput screening identifies compositions where these effects synergize.
generation.predicted_outcome: Candidate RHEAs will exhibit improved strength (by impeding dislocation slip via lattice distortion), enhanced ductility (through optimized phase stability and microstructural control), and lower density compared to traditional refractory alloys.
generation.baseline: Conventional RHEA compositions based solely on near-equiatomic refractory elements that may have high strength but suffer from brittleness and higher density.
generation.boundary: This method is expected to be most effective when the alloy system remains within refractory and low-weight element domains and when precise thermodynamic data or reliable CALPHAD models are available; extreme compositions or those with additional detrimental phases may not show the predicted trade-off optimization.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in strength, ductility, and weight reduction remain uncertain until validated experimentally; additionally, potential trade-offs (e.g., oxidation resistance) may require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a high-throughput computational study on a multi-element refractory alloy system to select candidate compositions predicted to have a disordered BCC matrix with low density. Synthesize a series of these candidate alloys, and then experimentally characterize their microstructure (via XRD and TEM), tensile properties (via stress-strain measurements at room and elevated temperatures), and density. Compare these results with those of conventional RHEAs.
measurements: Phase identification by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Mechanical testing: tensile strength, yield strength, and ductility (strain-to-failure) at room temperature and at elevated temperatures
Density measurements via Archimedes’ method or similar
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the candidate alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (beyond experimental uncertainty) in the combination of strength, ductility, and lower density compared to the conventional refractory HEA baseline, then the hypothesis that the high-throughput computational design method can reliably yield intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight RHEAs is falsified.

The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] .
